\chapter{Remaining FYP Plan}

\section{Remaining Scope}
Scope was baselined at the proposal and has not been reopened; what remains is what was already
committed but not yet built, plus two explicitly gated tiers (\path{docs/02-Requirements/
scope-boundary.md}). \textbf{Committed, not yet built:} the filesystem resource-event family
(static fields and system properties are built; filesystem is not); the cost-aware adaptive
search policy (ranked one-by-one ships now); rootless container sandboxing and the rest of the
security posture (Chapter 4's Table~\ref{ch4:tab:fr} and Appendix B's Table~\ref{appb:tab:security}
list exactly what is and is not built today); the test--resource graph beyond pairwise
edges; and NFR-2's clean-machine deployment check by a third party. \textbf{Gated, conditional
on the committed core:} Certificate-Driven Remediation (CDR) --- enabled only after the
committed core reaches its Final-1 exit criteria and ranking/explanation quality clears an
acceptance threshold on the development benchmark (\path{docs/07-Defense/decisions/
cdr-gated-module.md}) --- and the other optional tier (JUnit 5, Gradle, GitHub Checks,
issue-tracker export, a history dashboard, database/network resource adapters), each gated the
same way. If the team is behind at Final-1, the recorded cut order is CDR first, then
filesystem evidence (reduced to an opaque event), then the adaptive policy (ranked one-by-one
stays default); \textbf{the committed core end-to-end path is cut last, because it is the
project.}

\section{Remaining Modules and Features}
\textbf{Evaluation (M3, confident --- this is my own module).} Integrate at least one published
baseline (iFixFlakies minimiser, or RankFO) so claim B11 can move from ``partially'' to
measured; run the ablations already designed but not executed (resource-only, order-only,
static-only, no-cost-term, no-verification-reserve, the depth-sweep reporting both rank and
overlap-set size); build the held-out evaluation split (development / validation / untouched
projects, never split randomly by test); run the five user-acceptance tasks with the named
participant (SH1) and a substitute plan for the other two.

\textbf{Resource evidence (M1).} Iteration~1 extracts static-field and system-property evidence
for each polluter after the search has found it (Section~\ref{ch6:sec:m1}). What remains:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Evidence before the search.} To let Member~2 try evidence-backed candidates first
  (FR-4), the module must analyse every earlier test against the victim before the search, not
  only the polluters after it. On fastjson FJ-02 this took 148.3~s for all 722 candidates at
  depth~2 (\path{docs/evidence-m1.md}).
\item \textbf{The depth matrix at real scale}: depth used, false edges and time per pair on the
  benchmark projects, not only on two fastjson cases.
\item \textbf{Runtime evidence} as the fallback where static analysis cannot explain a case: an
  agent run on a temporary copy, only for the already reduced order (ADR-001).
\item \textbf{Filesystem paths} as the third resource family, with paths canonicalised so the
  same file is one resource, as the team's resource-family decision requires
  (\path{resource-family-boundaries.md} in \path{docs/07-Defense/decisions/}).
\item \textbf{The test--resource graph} beyond single polluter--victim pairs, and an explanation
  that can show more than the first edge when one test writes several fields, as with fastjson's
  time zone and locale.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Search, verification and CLI (M2).} Iteration 1's polluter search runs in the original
order with no ranking: \texttt{find\_polluter} accepts a \texttt{priority} list, but the command
never passes one. What remains: ranking through that hook, trying Member 1's evidence-backed
candidates first (FR-4), and then the cost-aware adaptive policy (\path{docs/00-Meta/roadmap.md},
Iteration 2); the container sandbox, rootless with the network disabled, resource limits,
verified cleanup and budgets beyond the 120\,s timeout (\path{docs/02-Requirements/
non-functional.md}); a human-readable certificate with the replay command, which closes the FR-6
gap recorded in Table~\ref{ch4:tab:fr}; a report for \texttt{NO\_SINGLE\_POLLUTER}, which needs a new schema reason
agreed with Member 3; running each test class's methods in one JUnit request, so
\texttt{@BeforeClass} runs once per class as under Surefire; and an installable
\texttt{flaketrace} command, which needs the packages renamed and the harness shipped as package
data (ADR-005), followed by the NFR-2 clean-install check.

\section{Implementation Plan}
My own near-term order: (1) wire one published baseline into \path{eval/baseline.py}'s existing
\texttt{OrderRunner} interface, reusing the class-first shuffle discipline already built and
tested; (2) extend the random-order comparison from the seeded fixture to the \texttt{idoft}
benchmark cases already listed (metadata-only today) in \path{eval/benchmark/manifest.json};
(3) build the held-out split once a second real project is cloned, per the leakage rule (a fix
commit used as an algorithm input cannot also be the oracle that judges it); (4) run the
acceptance tasks last, since they need a stable, demonstrable pipeline rather than one still
changing week to week.

Member 2's near-term order: (1) run one real project from the benchmark manifest end to end
through \texttt{py -m runner diagnose}, the FYP-1 Final outcome in \path{docs/08-MidEval/
iteration-plan.md}, first, because it will expose runner problems the seeded fixture cannot;
(2) the first deployment attempt in a container, the other part of that outcome; (3) ranking
through the \texttt{priority} hook with Member 1's evidence; (4) the human-readable certificate
and replay command; (5) the installable command and the NFR-2 check, a Final-2 requirement.
Step (1) also gives Member 3 the real-project data the held-out evaluation needs.

Member~1's near-term order: (1) the evidence-backed candidate order for Member~2's
\texttt{priority} hook, first, because Member~2's ranking step needs it; (2) the extractor on the
real benchmark project that Member~2 runs end to end, recording the depth matrix there; (3) runtime
evidence only for the cases step~2 shows static analysis cannot explain; (4) the filesystem family,
which the roadmap places in FYP-II's first phase; (5) the test--resource graph. Steps (1) and (2)
depend on Member~2's real-project run, and Member~3's held-out split decides which projects may be
used for development and which are kept for the final evaluation.

\section{Testing and Validation Plan}
The evaluation plan (\path{docs/05-Testing/evaluation-plan.md}) already defines what remains to
be measured, not just tested: eight research questions (RQ1--RQ6 committed, RQ7--RQ8 gated with
CDR), six baselines (random, one-by-one, iFixFlakies, RankFO/RankFL, Takuan, an oracle ceiling),
and a pre-registered failure condition --- a Verified certificate later shown wrong is the single
worst result the project can produce, more serious than any baseline underperforming. Testing
itself (does the implementation meet its requirements) stays continuous, as in Chapter 7;
evaluation (is the approach better under budget) and acceptance (would the intended users use
it) are what remain, and neither is started yet, stated plainly rather than implied as done.

\section{Deployment Plan}
Deployment is defined by NFR-2 (\path{docs/02-Requirements/non-functional.md}; claim E7 in
\path{docs/07-Defense/claims-ledger.md}): a third party installs FlakeTrace on a clean Linux
machine from the documentation, runs one frozen benchmark case, obtains the same certificate
class, replays the returned order, and removes every container and workspace it created. Tests
run under a two-phase network model: a networked dependency-fetch stage, then a test-execution
stage with the network disabled, as a separate container invocation, so test code is never
network-reachable even though the build was. This is a Final-2 exit requirement and was not
attempted in Iteration 1; the first step towards it, a deployment attempt in a container, is
part of the FYP-1 Final outcome.

\section{Expected Final Deliverables}
Per the roadmap's FYP-II-final exit evidence: frozen held-out results, a recorded acceptance
decision from the user tasks, a deployed release passing the NFR-2 clean-install check, and a
one-command reproducibility bundle. CDR ships only as V1 first, and only if its own gates (ranking
quality, explanation correctness, the committed core's Final-1 exit criteria) are met --- its
absence does not block any of the other deliverables, by design (``remove CDR and the product
still delivers its contribution,''
\path{docs/07-Defense/decisions/cdr-gated-module.md}).
